frase_gancho.texto: A clay smile more than a thousand years old that is still contagious.

puente_narrativo.texto: From joyful clay to solemn clay: look for the figure, almost life-size, of a seated woman with fixed eyes and serpents on her belt.

guion_corto.texto: This fired clay figure, about eighteen centimeters tall, is one of the so-called smiling faces of central Veracruz, made in the Remojadas area between the years six hundred and nine hundred of our era. Look at the face: the mouth wide open, the eyes half closed, and the front teeth filed, as if the figure were in the middle of a burst of laughter. It wears a rectangular headdress with relief designs and round ear ornaments, and its head is elongated, from an intentional deformation of the skull. In an ancient art that we tend to imagine as serious, these figures are a surprise. They have been interpreted as representing participants in rituals of music, dance, and trance. No one knows for certain why they smile, but their joy crosses the centuries.

guion_largo.texto:
After so many grave stones and stern faces, isn’t it a relief to find someone who is laughing? It is one of the surprises of Mesoamerican art: not everything was solemn.

Remojadas is a site in central Veracruz that gives its name to a clay tradition that lasted for centuries. These figures were made with the help of molds, touched up by hand, and painted. Many have been found, in tombs and in offerings, so they were not a rare object, but a much-loved image. On several, it is described that the pupils were marked with chapopote, the natural asphalt that seeps up in the region, a shiny black that gives the gaze an air of life.

Look at the teeth again: they are filed. You already saw that custom in the introduction hall, among the skulls with decorated teeth, when we talked about the body as a canvas. And the elongated head is the same deformation you saw in [Offering 4](mna_s08_ofrenda4_laventa) and that you will see again in the profile of [Pakal](mna_s09_mascara_pakal). This smile, then, carries all the fashion of its time: a molded skull, carved teeth, ear ornaments, and a headdress.

Why do they smile? There are several ideas. Some specialists think they represent people in ceremonies of music, dance, and trance, perhaps with fermented drinks or plants that alter consciousness. Others link them to the fertility cult and to festivals held to ask for good harvests. There are even those who imagine them as part of the games and celebrations that followed the serious rituals. No idea has been proven, and perhaps all of them hold something true. And they are not all alike: smiling figures have been described standing and seated, some with arms open, as if they were dancing.

Compare, too, with the first piece in the hall. The [Colossal Head](mna_s08_cabeza_colosal_6) commands respect; this smile invites you to come closer. They are two ways of imagining the human being, on the same coast and centuries apart. And there is another difference: clay, unlike stone, allowed many similar pieces to be made, so it is thought that these figures reached many more people. It was an art less of kings and more of everyone.

Here is a curious fact. In Veracruz, the artisans of this period also made animal figures with wheels, which look like toys. Yes, wheels: clay figures with little wheels are known, although they never had carts or draft animals to make use of them. Remember that in Oaxaca I told you about roads without wheels. This is the exception in miniature: the principle of the wheel was known, but it was not used to transport anything. An invention that stayed a toy.

On the upper floors you will get to know the Totonacs, who still live today in this region of Veracruz, and their Voladores (Flyers). A tradition that, like this smile, has survived the centuries.

So the next time someone says that the past was only blood and stone, remember this face. Someone, more than a thousand years ago, wanted to capture in clay the exact moment when a person laughs.

texto: Look at the smile: which teeth can you see, and how are they filed?
Notice the rectangular headdress and the round ear ornaments
Compare its expression with that of the Colossal Head

texto.pregunta: Myth: The ancient peoples of Mexico were always serious and solemn.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They laughed, too. The smiling faces show joy, music, and celebration within an art that we tend to imagine as grave.
